newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: GUATEMALANS BURY SOCCER DEAD AT PACKED CEMETERY.
newsitem.headline: GUATEMALANS BURY SOCCER DEAD AT PACKED CEMETERY.

text.p: Funerals jammed the main cemetery in Guatemala on Friday as impoverished families jostled to bury the dead from a soccer stadium disaster in which as many as 82 perished beneath an avalanche of bodies.

With funerals scheduled back-to-back all day, Guatemala City's main cemetery was packed with thousands of mourners, competing priests and funeral workers frantically checking off lists to ensure each coffin found its proper place.
Many were buried as they died, in a crush, and were packed at high speed into cheap vaults and bricked up by cemetery workers darting through the crowds with wheelbarrows of cement.

Most of the victims of the tragedy were poor, suffocated under a cascade of bodies in the cheap terraces of the Mateo Flores stadium just before Wednesday night's Guatemala-Costa Rica World Cup qualifier.
They were buried in flimsy wooden coffins in the so-called "niche area" on the fringes of the cemetery where bodies are slotted in for $15.
Angry and confused, mourners demanded better explanations from the government as to why the match turned into the worst stadium disaster in World Cup history.
One mother of nine said she had filed a suit demanding the arrest of officials she blames for the death of her husband, who was among the soccer fans trampled to death.
Sonia Vazquez, the widow of Samuel Chamale, said she presented a complaint in Guatemala City's criminal court, sending a copy to the media. A court clerk confirmed that a suit had been filed.

President Alvaro Arzu, addressing the nation in a solemn broadcast late on Thursday, pledged to find the cause of the deaths, naming a high-level commission, including the interior and health ministers, to report back within 15 days.
Arzu's government has initially laid the blame on a "brawl" by rowdy fans in the upper terraces of the stadium, which has a 47,000 capacity.
On radio talk shows, in streets and taxis, in lines at the cemetery, authorities were blamed for slapdash security at the match and the entry of hundreds of people with forged tickets.

"The police and the doorkeepers didn't have any control," said Lionel Ardon Rodriguez, a relative of a 13-year-old boy whose small coffin was slotted into the cemetery wall. "The authorities worry about how to get more people in to earn more money, but they don't care about security."
As hearses led columns of cars and rusty pick-up trucks snaking through the capital, the poverty of some of the mourners lent a wrenching aspect to the scene.

One group of casket bearers in tattered clothes were followed by a thin, elderly woman carrying a bag of cement on her head. Another inconsolable woman burying her husband and teenage son had to be gently pried from each casket before they were slid into the wall and cemented shut.
"Look how they left him," she said, referring to his battered body inside the coffin.
Many of the dead were maimed as they fell against the chain-link fence separating the stands from the playing field.

In response to the disaster, world soccer's governing body FIFA called on France to scrap the use of fences at its World Cup venues ahead of the 1998 finals. "Fences are for animals and prisoners, not football fans," FIFA general secretary Sepp Blatter said in Munich.
The exact death toll in Guatemala was still unclear. The government said 80 people died, but morgue officials said it rose to 82 after some injured died in the hospital.
Seeking to ease the suffering of the victims' families, Arzu announced that turnstile takings from the $7-a-head match would be seized and offered to them as compensation.

FIFA said Guatemala's next qualifying match against Trinidad and Tobago -- originally scheduled for next Friday -- had been postponed indefinitely, as had the aborted match against Costa Rica. Other matches would proceed as scheduled.
